Consider the system of linear differential equations above.
Find the unknown function $f(t)$ in the general solution to the system, shown below.
![](images/12/12ba5728836320b3d99d138507e5bb71e7f3a6bd2d93635443b7c26bb71a7ddd.svg)

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue $\lambda_1 = \textrm{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ![](images/fa/faa6212a47ec98f63248d7de696decaaba0b767e5771eef523ec1e9373051f21.svg)*" :question/worked-solution "We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix ![](images/d3/d33b2b3ad04f460f27c6f199b9f54ae327f48a96d1b3de8ce270e677440cac74.svg) 

We are given the eigenvalue $\lambda_1 = \textrm{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ![](images/9d/9d5190da8a9a59e2691c8ab16e366be20a14c6c7ce5b8f57986d4faa50cceb9e.svg)

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue $\lambda_2 = \overline{\lambda}_1$ is 
$\mathbf{v}_2 = \overline{\mathbf{v}}_1.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue $\lambda_1 = \textrm{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is
![](images/61/61c5ce70ef3272667953b10eb895ba8c480723399d5aeb96eae0e0f54064c1e1.svg)

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\text{i}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $\mathbf w_1$ and $\mathbf w_2$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t) = \cos{t} + \sin{t}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157449 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-b206ecea-c987-5f98-a428-5bb6722fc6f9"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157070 :question/problem "Solve the initial value problem

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue $\lambda_1 = 2\textrm{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ![](images/ae/ae46b58d986d4c703470adb45128c046e6e0e572ce92593a0661e990bcb1b661.svg)*" :question/worked-solution "We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix ![](images/ea/eaa7fa7c58b91792b295e853a01912a5ec45edda30f5de68f5e3952a73fae014.svg)

We are given the eigenvalue $\lambda_1 = 2\textrm{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ![](images/a2/a290109e5eb086926e15a1cffa9e11dd54b8843b3891068af7c322d10baa20de.svg)

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue $\lambda_2 = \overline{\lambda}_1$ is 
$\mathbf{v}_2 = \overline{\mathbf{v}}_1.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue $\lambda_1 = 2\textrm{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is
![](images/1e/1ec89bb86150c8b5002835d1f7a8f796f514e8c05f70303c833d13e922d5d390.svg)

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}](\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))+\text{i}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $\mathbf w_1$ and $\mathbf w_2$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of $c_1$ and $c_2$ using the initial condition ![](images/b2/b263aa33a22f008a8cc114136e985b5655cd0f097584c48311bb28eca256c2d2.svg) Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =1[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157450 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-a4f7c8d4-fcef-54e6-85b4-aab824651514"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157071 :question/problem "![](images/7a/7a0372520a2b91d2e3f928f808d210700f1076e44b94900244cc4af78e28cd24.svg)

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-ee5bc47e-f5eb-5ac3-a599-35150942e1b0" :question/id #uuid "ee5bc47e-f5eb-5ac3-a599-35150942e1b0" :question/math-academy-id "q-333911" :question/problem "$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}].$*" :question/worked-solution "We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ -6 & 3\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{3\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{3\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+2\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))+\text{i}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+2\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-dc7055a9-5fc1-5c31-8fe0-833c83e126c1"] :question/math-academy-id "q-334057" :question/problem "Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 5 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*" :question/worked-solution "We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 5 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].$

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}](\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\text{i}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$

"question-a4f7c8d4-fcef-54e6-85b4-aab824651514" :question/id #uuid "a4f7c8d4-fcef-54e6-85b4-aab824651514" :question/math-academy-id "q-334102" :question/problem "$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above.
Find the unknown function $f(t)$ in the general solution to the system, shown below.

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}f(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}
$$

*Hint: One of the eigenvalues of the matrix is ${\lambda }_{1}=3+\text{i}.$*" :question/worked-solution "We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given that the eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=3+\text{i}.$ 

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For ${\lambda }_{1}=3+\text{i},$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} & -1 \\ 1 & -\text{i}\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\text{i} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3+\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(3+\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(3+\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\text{i}({e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\ {e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}({e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-bfe17ed2-090f-567a-b946-9998b5018bd8"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} :question/math-academy-id "q-334220" :question/problem "Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].

*Hint: One of the eigenvalues of the matrix is ${\lambda }_{1}=3+4\text{i}.$*" :question/worked-solution "We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given that the eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=3+4\text{i}.$ 

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For ${\lambda }_{1}=3+4\text{i},$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-4\text{i} & -8 \\ 2 & -4\text{i}\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2\text{i} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3+4\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(3+4\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(3+4\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\text{i}(2{e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)) \\ {e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}({e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t))\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-46d5e602-1b49-5a34-81a0-cd7ca46f078e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id We are given that the eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+3\text{i}.$ 

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+3\text{i},$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-3\text{i} & 3 \\ -3 & -3\text{i}\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & \text{i} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+3\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(-2+3\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(-2+3\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+\text{i}(-{e}^{-2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\ {e}^{-2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}({e}^{-2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}](\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\text{i}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

We are given that the eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=3+\text{i}.$ 

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For ${\lambda }_{1}=3+\text{i},$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} & -1 \\ 1 & -\text{i}\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\text{i} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3+\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(3+\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(3+\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\text{i}({e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\ {e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}({e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that the eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=3+4\text{i}.$ 

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For ${\lambda }_{1}=3+4\text{i},$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-4\text{i} & -8 \\ 2 & -4\text{i}\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2\text{i} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3+4\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(3+4\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(3+4\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\text{i}(2{e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)) \\ {e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}({e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t))\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$

$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =-2[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =-2[\begin{aligned}5\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-b206ecea-c987-5f98-a428-5bb6722fc6f9" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-72091d3f-d275-5236-8df0-f9e9952f0d22" :answer-field/id #uuid *Hint: One of the eigenvalues of the matrix is ${\lambda }_{1}=3+4\text{i}.$*"] ["question-421de516-3253-5c4d-bb0f-0143da489cf9" :question/worked-solution "We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given that the eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=3+4\text{i}.$ 

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For ${\lambda }_{1}=3+4\text{i},$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-4\text{i} & -8 \\ 2 & -4\text{i}\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2\text{i} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3+4\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(3+4\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(3+4\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\text{i}(2{e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)) \\ {e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}({e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t))\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}

:question/problem "Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: One of the eigenvalues of the matrix is ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+3\text{i}.$*"] ["question-ff1d5823-2f0a-574c-b322-55ba80787b34" :question/worked-solution "We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given that the eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+3\text{i}.$ 

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+3\text{i},$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-3\text{i} & 3 \\ -3 & -3\text{i}\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & \text{i} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+3\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(-2+3\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(-2+3\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+\text{i}(-{e}^{-2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\ {e}^{-2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}({e}^{-2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-ff1d5823-2f0a-574c-b322-55ba80787b34" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-47bc44df-a5cf-5002-aff0-ebeea9327157" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -5 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))+\text{i}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 26 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-5\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*" :question/worked-solution "We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 26 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-5\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1-5\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{5\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1-5\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{5\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-5\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)-5\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t))+\text{i}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)-5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)-5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)-5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}-5{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =1[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}]+0[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)-5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186391373 :question/id #uuid "0f26b8b6-ea22-55f9-adb9-e96204409f88" :question/math-academy-id "q-334053"} {:db/id 17592186391380 :question/id #uuid $$

17592186158396 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158469 :tutorial/content "For a $2 \times 2$ matrix differential equation

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),
$$

 

we know that if $A$ has distinct eigenvalues, the general solution is

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\color{black}\mathbf{v}_1} e^{{\color{black}\lambda_1} t} + c_2{\color{black}\mathbf{v}_2} e^{{\color{black}\lambda_2} t}.
$$

This formula works even when the eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \lambda_2$ are complex. However, using it directly requires working with complex exponentials, which can be cumbersome.

A more direct method is to find just *one* of the complex solutions, say $\mathbf x_1(t) = \mathbf{v}_1 e^{{\color{black}\lambda_1} t},$ and separate it into its *real and imaginary parts*.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & ={v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t} \\  & ={{{w}_{1}(t)}_{⏟}}_{\text{Real Part}}\,+\,\text{i}\,\,\,{{{w}_{2}(t)}_{⏟}}_{\text{Imaginary Part}}\end{aligned}
$$

The general *real-valued* solution is then a linear combination of these two parts:

$$
\mathbf x(t) = c_1 \mathbf w_1(t) + c_2 \mathbf w_2(t)
$$

**Note:** This method may seem surprising. Why can we construct the general solution using only *one* of the complex solutions, $\mathbf x_1(t)?$

The reason is that the second solution, $\mathbf x_2(t),$ doesn't provide any new information. For a real matrix $A,$ the complex eigenvalues and eigenvectors come in *conjugate pairs*, which means $\mathbf x_2(t)$ is simply the complex conjugate of $\mathbf x_1(t).$

Since $\mathbf x_2(t) = \mathbf w_1 (t) - \textrm{i} \, \mathbf w_2(t),$ it is also a linear combination of the real and imaginary parts of $\mathbf x_1(t).$

To build our general solution, we just need two *linearly independent* real solutions. The key facts are the following:

- For a system with complex eigenvalues, the real part $\mathbf w_1(t)$ and the imaginary part $\mathbf w_2(t)$ are *always* linearly independent.

- Since they are two linearly independent solutions, they can form the basis for the general solution.

So, we can use them directly and bypass the need to work with $\mathbf x_2(t)$ at all.

Let's see a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "a93ff6d6-1eb0-5e42-8b69-ae73fc891839" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4283 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid \mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\color{black}\mathbf{v}_1} e^{{\color{black}\lambda_1} t} + c_2{\color{black}\mathbf{v}_2} e^{{\color{black}\lambda_2} t}.
$$

This formula works even when the eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \lambda_2$ are complex. However, using it directly requires working with complex exponentials, which can be cumbersome.

A more direct method is to find just *one* of the complex solutions, say $\mathbf x_1(t) = \mathbf{v}_1 e^{{\color{black}\lambda_1} t},$ and separate it into its *real and imaginary parts*.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & ={v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t} \\  & ={{{w}_{1}(t)}_{⏟}}_{\text{Real Part}}\,+\,\text{i}\,\,\,{{{w}_{2}(t)}_{⏟}}_{\text{Imaginary Part}}\end{aligned}
$$

The general *real-valued* solution is then a linear combination of these two parts:

$$
\mathbf x(t) = c_1 \mathbf w_1(t) + c_2 \mathbf w_2(t)
$$

**Note:** This method may seem surprising. Why can we construct the general solution using only *one* of the complex solutions, $\mathbf x_1(t)?$

The reason is that the second solution, $\mathbf x_2(t),$ doesn't provide any new information. For a real matrix $A,$ the complex eigenvalues and eigenvectors come in *conjugate pairs*, which means $\mathbf x_2(t)$ is simply the complex conjugate of $\mathbf x_1(t).$

Since $\mathbf x_2(t) = \mathbf w_1 (t) - \textrm{i} \, \mathbf w_2(t),$ it is also a linear combination of the real and imaginary parts of $\mathbf x_1(t).$

To build our general solution, we just need two *linearly independent* real solutions. The key facts are the following:

- For a system with complex eigenvalues, the real part $\mathbf w_1(t)$ and the imaginary part $\mathbf w_2(t)$ are *always* linearly independent.

- Since they are two linearly independent solutions, they can form the basis for the general solution.

So, we can use them directly and bypass the need to work with $\mathbf x_2(t)$ at all.

techniques used throughout modern physics. Building on the analytical framework established in the first course, students study orthogonality, multivariable integration, vector calculus theorems, and advanced methods for differential equations.

These tools provide the mathematical foundation for analyzing electromagnetic fields, wave phenomena, dynamical systems, and statistical models encountered in advanced physics courses." 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1009 "The course begins with the theory of projections in inner product spaces. Students study norms, inner products, orthogonality, and orthogonal complements in vector spaces over the real and complex numbers. Techniques such as orthogonal projections, the Gram–Schmidt process, and QR factorization allow vectors to be decomposed into orthogonal components. These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.
Students then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.
Applications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.
The course then develops multivariable integration in three dimensions. Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.
Students next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Concepts such as circulation, flux, and path independence lead to the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Green’s theorem, the divergence theorem, and Stokes’ theorem. These results form the mathematical framework underlying conservation laws and the differential and integral formulations of electromagnetic theory.
Applications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization. Students analyze motion using vector-valued functions, apply Newton’s second law to systems in the plane, and study work–energy relationships. Multiple integrals are used to compute mass, centers of mass, moments of inertia, and other physical quantities.
The course then returns to differential equations, extending earlier techniques to systems of linear differential equations. Students analyze dynamical systems using eigenvalues, phase portraits, and matrix methods, which appear in models of interacting systems such as coupled oscillators or predator–prey dynamics.
Laplace transforms are introduced as a powerful tool for solving linear differential equations with discontinuous inputs or initial conditions. Boundary value problems and Fourier series are then developed, providing mathematical techniques used to solve differential equations describing heat flow, vibrating strings, wave propagation, and other physical phenomena.
The course concludes with numerical methods for differential equations and advanced probability topics. Students analyze the accuracy and stability of numerical schemes used in computational physics and study multivariate probability distributions and the central limit theorem, which appear in
